summary: Deep technical session investigating intermittent p99 spikes observed when Catalyst routes streaming requests through the multi-NIC VPC edge. We covered how quantization changes execution paths, how KV cache hot-shards and network IRQ/coalescing cause tail amplification, and tradeoffs between streaming vs non-streaming fallbacks. Agreed to run targeted microbenchmarks single-vs-dual NIC and share benchmark spreadsheet; customer to provide traffic profile.
topics: streaming vs non-streaming fallbacks and heuristics
multi-NIC VPC edge and SR-IOV / RSS impact
KV cache hot-shard and sharding strategies
on-prem vs VPC network stack differences and NIC interrupt moderation
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-07
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 78 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood Solutions), Ravi (Catalyst Platform), Sofia (Catalyst SRE), Evan (Catalyst VP Eng), Lena (Catalyst Security)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for carving out time. We're here to dig into the p99 noise you're seeing at the edge with streaming requests. Quick check - is this the spike that shows up mostly during deploys or steady traffic?

[00:18] Ravi Patel: It's mostly steady traffic, um spikes are kinda random but they show up more when we have heavier KV cache miss rates. We have a dual-NIC host for the edge proxies, SR-IOV is enabled.

[00:35] Diego Alvarez: okay, great. That combination - dual NIC + SR-IOV + KV miss fanout can produce amplification. We'll want to separate concerns: network level (NIC queues/irq), runtime (quantized kernel path), and KV layer hot-shard.

[00:50] Sofia Martinez: we also saw that when you switch models to int8 quant the p95 stays fine but p99 gets worse. thought quant would always help.

[01:05] Diego Alvarez: yeah that's a really important observation. Quantization changes the execution path: some kernels use vectorized int8 solvers that are faster on average but have occasional cache-line dependent branching and different memory patterns for KV cache prefetching. That can interact badly with streaming because streaming keeps small prefixes alive across many requests, so any jitter in the int8 path can push a few requests into the tail.

[01:32] Evan Liu: can you explain streaming fallthrough? we use streaming for UX reasons but if it's causing spikes maybe we need to fallback to non-streaming in some situations.

[01:45] Maya Chen: Absolutely. With Redwood's runtime we have a streaming-first path that emits tokens as they're ready. There's a fallthrough to non-streaming (buffered) when latency destabilizes or when a compatible fallback model is selected. The heuristics look at token throughput variance, queue depth, and KV miss ratio. In practice, sometimes the fallback triggers too late when p99 is already affected.

[02:10] Ravi Patel: our edge is multi-NIC. we run control traffic on nic0 and model traffic on nic1 but there's still a lot of shared interrupts and lock contention in the kernel. could that create long-tail jitter?

[02:25] Diego Alvarez: yes. With SR-IOV you can isolate queues, but unless RSS and interrupt moderation are tuned, you can get unfair distribution of flows across vfs. Also NAPI coalescing can create 1-2ms bursts. At the p99 level those bursts show up. We recommend measuring irq-affinity, RSS hashing, and disabling adaptive coalescing during the test.

[02:52] Sofia Martinez: what about MTU? we run jumbo frames but not sure all the path supports it.

[02:58] Diego Alvarez: mismatched MTU can cause fragmentation and increase serialization time at the host — not usually huge for token-level traffic but can exacerbate bustiness when combined with retransmits. Good to verify with iperf and tracepath.

[03:15] Lena Korhonen: security question - if we run on-prem with our HSM and KMS, does Redwood still do streaming? and does encryption increase latency?

[03:25] Maya Chen: streaming works with Private deployments and KMS/HSM integrations; encryption adds a few ms for each key unwrap depending on HSM latency, but it doesn't explain multi-ms p99 spikes unless the KMS itself is throttled. We also log audit events; we can throttle them or batch logs to reduce tail effects.

[03:45] Sophie (sic) - uh Sofia: there's also a KV shadowing setup - we shadow traffic to a cold-onprem cache and that sometimes causes timeouts that propagate upstream.

[03:55] Diego Alvarez: that can definitely amplify tails. If a shadow path blocks on a slow response, depending on your proxy config (sync vs async shadowing), it may add head-of-line blocking. Recommend ensuring shadowing is async and early-exit on slow shadow responses.

[04:12] Evan Liu: curious about the quant kernels - is the int8 path single-threaded or multithreaded? we saw core pinning differences.

[04:22] Diego Alvarez: there are two things: model kernels (GEMM) run on GPU/accelerator if you're using Redwood Dedicated or on quantized CPU kernels if running on-prem CPU. For CPU quantized paths, the runtime may use different thread pools and memory strides. Sometimes thread pool contention with our batching thread causes latency spikes for the first token in a batch. We can tweak the thread-affinity to pin batching workers away from NIC IRQ threads.

[04:55] Ravi Patel: any quick wins we can try this week?

[05:00] Diego Alvarez: yes — three quick tests: 1) run iperf/packetgen to compare single-NIC vs dual-NIC throughput and jitter, 2) run a 1k qps synthetic workload with int8 vs fp16 and capture p95/p99 and perf counters, 3) temporarily disable shadowing to see if p99 improves. We'll capture histograms.

[05:28] Maya Chen: we'll put together a benchmark spreadsheet template (we'll share link) so we can compare apples-to-apples. If you can produce the traffic profile we'll pre-populate it.

[05:40] Sofia Martinez: how do we interpret p99 increases that only affect streaming? are there heuristics to degrade earlier?

[05:48] Diego Alvarez: streaming emits partial tokens continuously — so the runtime keeps an open connection and small state. If a host hiccups for 10-30ms it impacts multiple in-flight streams. A non-streaming buffered response isolates that burst to a single request. Heuristic-wise, we recommend: set a conservative batching window (e.g., 8-12ms) for streaming fallbacks, add a secondary SLO at p99 for streaming endpoints, and configure the runtime to preemptively buffer if KV miss ratio > X%. We'll share exact threshold suggestions in the note.

[06:20] Ravi Patel: question about KV sharding: we shard by user id right now, but sometimes we see hotspotting for a handful of heavy accounts.

[06:32] Diego Alvarez: you can mitigate with consistent hashing + virtual shards and client-side request routing that spreads hot keys. Also consider local LRU for hot prefixes at the edge proxy to cut the roundtrip. Prefix caching helps a lot for streaming UX.

[06:50] Evan Liu: any effect from our load balancer healthchecks? we use 10s health checks that sometimes run into borderline thresholds.

[06:58] Diego Alvarez: aggressive healthchecks can cause flapping that redistributes traffic and create cold caches. Make them slightly less frequent or add gradual draining to avoid knee-jerk backfills.

[07:12] Sofia Martinez: can we instrument more? we currently have token-level histograms but not NIC-level alignment.

[07:20] Maya Chen: Diego will provide an instrumentation checklist: NIC irq metrics, NAPI backlog, per-core runqueue, KV latency breakdown, runtime batching distributions, and token emission timestamps. That will help correlate events.

[07:38] Ravi Patel: when you said earlier about disabling adaptive coalescing — is that safe in prod?

[07:45] Diego Alvarez: it's a diagnostic step. For short windows in a staging environment it's fine. In prod you'd want to tune interrupt moderation parameters rather than fully disable. We'll propose safe knob ranges.

[08:00] Maya Chen: okay switching gears, let's talk about fallback routing — you mentioned sometimes the runtime falls back to a smaller model automatically?

[08:08] Diego Alvarez: yes, Redwood Smart Routing has policies to route to cheaper model variants when latency or capacity constraints occur. But routing decisions need stable signals; a single noisy spike should not trigger a global fallback. We recommend smoothing windows and adding hysteresis to avoid oscillation.

[08:28] Evan Liu: are there examples of quantization causing non-deterministic latencies?

[08:34] Diego Alvarez: yes — int8 microkernels can introduce data-dependent loads and micro-benchmark variance. Also some BLAS libraries enable different blocksizes that cause microsecond-level jitter. The result is benign for average latency but shows up at p99. We handle some of this in compile-time kernel selection but in on-prem setups you may have older microcode or DVFS that increases variance.

[08:58] Sofia Martinez: hmm DVFS. our staging uses performance governor but prod is ondemand. should we force performance?

[09:06] Diego Alvarez: for strict p99 SLOs, performance governor reduces variance. It's a tradeoff with power. For p99-sensitive endpoints we often recommend performance mode and power budgeting elsewhere.

[09:22] Maya Chen: quick note on measurement: are you reporting p99 from load balancer logs or from Redwood per-request traces?

[09:30] Ravi Patel: load balancer + internal proxy metrics. there's slight mismatch between them.

[09:36] Diego Alvarez: ok capture both and align clocks. Load balancer will include network egress time; runtime traces isolate server compute time. Correlating the two often reveals whether the tail is network or compute.

[09:50] Evan Liu: any particular experiments on batching windows for streaming? we tried 2ms and 20ms and both felt suboptimal.

[09:58] Diego Alvarez: try a dynamic window: start at 4-6ms and grow if queue depth signals increase. Also consider token-prefetch heuristics to ensure the first tokens are not stalled waiting for a large batch. For streaming the first-token latency matters a lot for UX.

[10:18] Sofia Martinez: i want to capture an action item — I'll export the VPC flow logs and topology by Friday.

[10:24] Maya Chen: perfect. Diego, can you summarize the recommended triage order?

[10:30] Diego Alvarez: 1) isolate network: run iperf, irq-affinity, RSS and verify MTU; 2) isolate runtime: run int8 vs fp16 microbench with empty KV and with KV miss fanout; 3) disable async shadowing and re-measure; 4) tune streaming window and fallback thresholds; 5) if still present, run on-prem test with Redwood engineers to capture perf counters.

[10:58] Ravi Patel: about the on-prem run - what's required from our side? rack access, HSM connectivity?

[11:05] Maya Chen: ideally a staging rack with network mirror and access to logs, plus KMS test credentials for encrypted path. We'll provide a checklist and the test harness.

[11:20] Diego Alvarez: i'll also include a sample perfctl script to capture runqueue latencies, irq counts, NIC stats, and glibc malloc metrics — those often reveal the surprising root causes.

[11:35] Evan Liu: curious - do you think the problem is more likely network or runtime?

[11:40] Diego Alvarez: my bet is network+KV interplay. The kernel coalescing plus hot KV fanout triggers a small set of threads to stall and that cascades into streaming tails. But we need the data.

[11:52] Maya Chen: okay, let's recap next steps briefly. Diego will run NIC tests and provide instrument checklist; Maya to share benchmark template and quant note; Catalyst to provide topologies and traffic profile; schedule on-prem test week of 4/20.

[12:10] Ravi Patel: thank you — very actionable. any docs you can share on the runtime heuristics?

[12:17] Maya Chen: yes i'll attach the Redwood streaming fallthrough heuristics doc and our Optimize quantization playbook. also will include a short note on recommended kernel tunables.

[12:30] Sofia Martinez: and please put the benchmark spreadsheet link in the calendar invite.

[12:35] Maya Chen: will do. thanks everyone. we'll follow up in the thread with artifacts.

[12:40] (call ends)
